# Exposing a local runtime: routes, and the protocol facts that constrain them Companion to §11. Everything here fronts a service that stays bound to `127.0.0.1`; none of it rebinds one. ## Route comparison | Route | Auth strength | Attack surface | Cost to set up | Client offline | |---|---|---|---|---| | Mesh VPN node share (Tailscale/WireGuard) | device identity + network ACL, deny-by-default once policies are written | only the shared machine; a shared node is quarantined by default (inbound only) and carries no tags/groups/subnets | low; the recipient needs the client and an account | good: recovery does not depend on a public entrypoint | | SSH tunnel (`ssh -N -L 8765:127.0.0.1:8765 …`) | strong (host key + public key) | needs SSH reachability to this box | one command | medium: reconnect is manual | | Public tunnel (Cloudflare Tunnel / ngrok) | "whoever knows the URL" unless an identity layer is stacked on it | the endpoint is genuinely public; a misconfiguration is a bare service | medium; cloudflared dials out, so inbound can stay closed | good | | mTLS | strong; a token can be bound to the certificate (RFC 8705) | you own issuance, revocation and rotation | medium-high (PKI) | same as HTTP | | Reverse proxy + OAuth | strong, user-level identity, one front door | a bypassable proxy is the hole; a wrong JWT check is no auth | medium-high | good, but session expiry interrupts long tasks | **A mesh VPN's real trap:** on Tailscale, if you write no `acls` section the default is *allow all*, not deny — write the policy explicitly. Node sharing is the narrower tool for a single recipient and strips their view to just that machine. ## Pick by the client's answers - Third party, arbitrary network, willing to install a client → **mesh VPN node share**, then serve the app on the tailnet with the target still `http://127.0.0.1`. - Third party, arbitrary network, will install nothing → **public tunnel plus an identity layer** (an access-control fronting, or service tokens); this is the only route where a stranger's browser is the client, so the identity layer is mandatory, not optional. - You, on another of your own devices → mesh VPN, or an SSH tunnel if you only need it now. - Must keep working while the host is off → no thin client; it has to be an isomorphic runtime on an always-on host, with only the knowledge layer shared. ## Free routes, and the facts that decide between them When there is no domain and no budget, the mesh-VPN node share is the whole answer — and the specifics that make it usable are all quoted from vendor documentation, not inferred: - **Sharing is available on all plans**, and the recipient does **not** need a Tailscale account with the same email — they accept a single-use invite link (unused links expire after 30 days). - **A shared machine is quarantined by default**: it *"can receive incoming connections … but cannot start connections"*, and sharing strips tags, groups and subnet routes from the recipient's view. This is the property that makes it the narrow tool rather than "let them into my tailnet". - **`tailscale serve` proxies only `http://127.0.0.1`** — *"Note that only http://127.0.0.1 is supported for proxies."* That single restriction is why the loopback bind survives exposure and why this pairs cleanly with the never-rebind rule above. A public tunnel provider, by contrast, asks for the target of your choice but requires a domain on their platform to publish a named app; their no-domain "quick" tunnels are documented as **testing and development only**, with no SLA. - **Do not use Funnel for a third party.** Vendor docs say it *"doesn't work with other Tailscale features like … access controls"*, that Funnel traffic (unlike Serve) **carries no identity headers**, and that it is limited to ports 443/8443/10000. That combination hands "who may connect" entirely back to the application, which is the opposite of what this route is chosen for. - **No transport removes "the host must be on".** Serve/Funnel, node sharing and the tunnel providers all state it as a shared precondition: reachable only while the device is online and the service is running. There is no built-in queueing or offline fallback, so a nightly power-down is an availability statement to the user — never a thing to engineer around with a thin client. - **A tunnel's own health indicator is not a service check.** Cloudflare documents that `Healthy` *"confirms only that cloudflared connects to Cloudflare … does not test the route's service or the local origin"*; the same over-claim applies to any provider dashboard. If the operator needs to know the service is up, that check has to run locally. ## Protocol facts that change the design A2A, v1.0 (published 2026-03-12). The normative artefact is `spec/a2a.proto`; the website JSON is a build product. Agent Card is mandatory and its well-known URI is `/.well-known/agent-card.json`; servers MUST provide it, and it SHOULD NOT carry internal implementation details. Clients MUST send an `A2A-Version` header on every request. Long tasks have three delivery mechanisms — polling (the documented choice when the client sits behind a restrictive firewall), SSE streaming (`SubscribeToTask` can re-attach after a disconnect), and push-notification webhooks, which require the client to be reachable *inbound* and oblige the server to validate the webhook URL against SSRF (private ranges named in the spec). Production MUST encrypt transport. **Authorization is explicitly left to the implementation**, and the enterprise documentation states the payload carries no user/client identity — identity is established at the HTTP layer, which is why one peer token per machine is the shape the protocol implies rather than a convention. `https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification` · `https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/topics/enterprise-ready/` · `https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/topics/streaming-and-async/` · `https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/releases/tag/v1.0.0` MCP, revision 2026-07-28, was a breaking rewrite: protocol-level sessions and `Mcp-Session-Id` are gone, `initialize` is gone (`server/discover` is mandatory instead), and SSE resumability/ re-delivery was removed — so "reconnect and replay missed events" is no longer a protocol responsibility, and most advice written before this revision is wrong. Two standard transports remain: `stdio` and Streamable HTTP (HTTP+SSE is deprecated). Streamable HTTP servers MUST check the `Origin` header against DNS rebinding, and locally-run servers SHOULD bind `127.0.0.1` only — **a stdio server (what this install runs) is therefore already the conservative choice**, and the authorization chapter is normative down to token audience (resource server per RFC 9728, RFC 8707 resource indicators, never pass a client token upstream), which is a far stricter posture than A2A's. Do not port one protocol's authorization rules onto the other. `https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog` · `https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/streamable-http` · `https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/authorization` · `https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/security_best_practices` ## Facts about this box to re-verify before claiming anything is remote-usable - `ss -tlnp` is the check. Last measured, every application port was `127.0.0.1`; the only non-loopback listener was the WSL DNS stub. "Another machine can already reach it" is almost always false here. - An agent card that answers `200` without a token is public by default — the check for whether a surface is protected, not evidence that the runtime is ready for visitors. - The KB gateway's downstream is loopback too, so the shared store is a *same-machine* service, not a cross-machine one, and `/mnt/d` is the same machine's Windows side rather than a network path. - A git remote is not a backup for the runtime state: only the tracked artifact tree is pushed, while audit/event/token files live outside it in the state directory. ## Standing it up: the app-side half The route table chooses the transport. Fronting an *agent runtime* has an ordering rule of its own, because the gate is switched on by the URL rather than by the tunnel. - **Order: credentials → `public_url` → tunnel.** Declaring a non-loopback `public_url` is what engages the dashboard auth gate, and the runtime then **fails closed at startup** when no auth provider is configured. So: write the provider's credentials into that profile's `.env` first (`USERNAME` / `PASSWORD` or `PASSWORD_HASH` / `SECRET` — the `SECRET` is the session-signing key), then set `public_url`, then open the tunnel. A tunnel opened first (or in the same breath) leaves the backend answering with the owner's authority for the length of that window. Reverse the order and the failure mode is loud and confusing: the service refuses to start at all. - **`public_url` must be the exact `Host` the browser sends** — it is matched verbatim (also as a WebSocket `Origin`), so a wrong MagicDNS name produces rejected requests, not a helpful error. - **A loopback session token is deliberately not a remote credential.** The documented reason is that a non-loopback `public_url` "prevents the local SPA session token from becoming a remote authentication mechanism". Tell the operator to expect a **sign-in** (username/password or OAuth), not a token to paste — and to set the signing secret, or every restart logs the guest out. - **Probe the gate state, not the config.** `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:/api/status` reports `auth_required` and `auth_providers`; acceptance is `auth_required=true` with the provider listed. Measured on an unconfigured backend: `auth_required=false, providers=[]` — that is the state in which the port is open to anyone who can reach it, so read it *before* exposing. - **No `trusted_proxies` entry is needed when the terminator is on loopback** (loopback proxies are trusted automatically); only a terminator in another host or container has to be listed. ### Which server process to front, and what "working" looks like - **`serve` and `dashboard` are two surfaces sharing one server — pick by client, before exposing.** `serve` is the headless backend the desktop app connects to: it sets `headless_backend=True` and exports `HERMES_SERVE_HEADLESS=1`, which makes `mount_spa()` disable the web UI *even when a build exists on disk*. `dashboard` serves the same JSON-RPC/WS API **plus** the UI. So the desktop client works against either, a browser works only against `dashboard`, and one process on one port is enough for both. For a unit: `hermes dashboard --host 127.0.0.1 --port

--no-open --skip-build`. `--skip-build` covers the **web** assets only: the chat page additionally runs the bundled TUI, so a tenant on a read-only code tree must have that bundle pinned prebuilt or the page reports *Chat unavailable* and the journal shows a permission error inside the app tree — see `references/tenant-isolation.md` → "A read-only code tree breaks everything that builds on demand". - **A JSON body where an HTML page was expected is the tell.** Wrong surface, not a broken gate: the browser reaches the login, authenticates, and then gets `{"error":"Headless backend (hermes serve): web UI disabled — use \`hermes dashboard\` for the browser UI."}` with HTTP 200 — nothing in the tunnel or the auth config is at fault, and no amount of re-checking `tailscale serve status` will show it. - **Probe the surface, not the config, to declare the entry path done.** Unauthenticated `/` must be a `302` to `/login?next=%2F`; `/login` must return `200` with a sign-in page carrying a password field; `/api/auth/me` must be `401`; `/api/status` must report the provider. Run these with the public `Host` header too (`curl -H "Host: " http://127.0.0.1:/...`) — the auth gate is engaged by `public_url`, so the loopback request is already gated, and this checks the host match without needing the guest's machine. - **The credentials in a profile's `.env` are loaded by a standalone service** — verified on a unit with no `EnvironmentFile=`, where the gate engaged and `/api/status` listed the provider. No unit edit is needed for the password provider; do not add an `EnvironmentFile` "to be safe" and then believe it was what made the gate work. - **The first `serve --https` has a minute-long TLS gap that looks like a failed step.** The certificate is provisioned on demand via ACME DNS-01 (it writes a `_acme-challenge` record first), so between the `serve` command and the certificate landing every request fails and the operator reads it as "step 4 failed". Check `journalctl -u tailscaled` for `health(warnable=tls-cert-pending): error: Fetching TLS certificate via ACME` followed by `got cert` — then tell them to retry, not to re-edit anything. The certificate is cached, so later restarts of the same name are immediate, and `tailscale status --json` reporting `CertDomains: null` before the first `serve` is expected rather than a misconfiguration. ### WSL specifics when the service lives inside WSL2 - **Run the mesh client inside WSL *or* on Windows — never both.** Vendor docs: traffic from WSL over the Windows host's Tailscale "will not work", because the packets cannot nest; the WSL interface MTU (1280) is also below what the daemon wants and is raised only when it detects WSL. If it later gets installed on the Windows side as well, the WSL copy has to come out. - **`tailscale serve --https` requires HTTPS certificates enabled for the tailnet** in the admin console before it will mint one. The tell that it is still off: `tailscale status --json` reports `CertDomains: null`. - **Hand the operator a sudo-free CLI**: `sudo tailscale set --operator=$USER`, otherwise every `serve` invocation needs root. - **Identify the node by tailnet IP when sharing it.** A WSL node commonly inherits the Windows hostname and appears in the machine list as a duplicate or `-1` entry. - `tailscale serve status` reporting **"No serve config"** is the honest state after a successful install + login: installing, logging in, and exposing are three separate steps, and the first two are not evidence of the third.

# Isolating a second tenant on the same machine Companion to §11. `references/remote-exposure.md` covers how a second party *reaches* a service; this covers what stops them reading everything else once they are running on the box. ## Why a profile, and why the same user, are not isolation - Hermes' own docs, on profiles: a profile is a separate Hermes *home*, and **"Profiles do not sandbox the agent … on the default local terminal backend the agent still has the same filesystem access as your user account. A profile does not stop it from accessing folders outside the profile directory."** The same page separately says **"SOUL.md can guide the model, but it does not enforce a workspace boundary."** Use these two sentences verbatim when writing the design up — they are the honest framing, and they come from the vendor rather than from you. - The Linux kernel says the same about the OS: *"a single user is able to examine the memory and running state of any of their processes"* (Yama LSM docs). Consequence: **`chmod 600` on a secret is not protection from a sibling process owned by the same user**, and `/proc//environ` is readable across processes of one user. File permissions only start meaning something across *users*. - systemd's own manual calls environment variables **unsuitable for passing secrets** (exposed to unprivileged clients over D-Bus, propagated down the process tree including across setuid boundaries) and names `LoadCredential=` instead. - systemd also gates a large block of hardening to system services only — `RootImageOptions=`, `RootEphemeral=`, `DynamicUser=`, capabilities, and assorted MAC/sandbox options are documented as **"only available for system services and is not supported for services running in per-user instances"**. A `systemd --user` unit therefore cannot be hardened properly, so "stay on the user manager" is a structural decision, not a config oversight. ArchWiki states it plainly: user units *"can not be hardened or sandboxed properly"*. ## The recipe 1. **A separate OS user for the tenant runtime.** Nothing else in this recipe matters without it. 2. **Its `HERMES_HOME` outside the owner's home**, owned by that user (`/var/lib//.hermes`). Moving the profile out is what lets you hide the owner's home wholesale. 3. **Read-only access to the code, granted narrowly.** Two paths, not one: the app tree *and* the virtualenv (the `hermes` entry point is a script whose shebang names the venv's python). Grant with `setfacl` rather than loosening the directory mode. 4. **The credential as a root-owned file, injected by systemd:** `LoadCredential=:/etc//…` (mode 600, root) plus `Environment=_TOKENS=%d/` — `%d` expands to the unit's private credentials directory, so the *path* is in the environment and the *secret* never is. Verified workable when the credential reader honors a path-shaped override (here: `INTELLIGENCE_TOKENS`). To avoid depending on specifier expansion inside `Environment=` at all, the literal resolved path `/run/credentials/.service/` is equivalent for a system unit. Note that the file under `/etc` stays root-only: the tenant reads the *injected copy*, so every reader must be pointed at the credentials directory — point a client at the `/etc` source and it fails to open a file it is not allowed to see. 5. **A model credential for the tenant runtime — it cannot inherit the owner's.** A second OS user with its own `HERMES_HOME` cannot read the owner's `.env` or `auth.json`, so a tenant profile seeded from the owner's env file may arrive with no provider key at all: the first turn answers `agent init failed: No usable credentials found for provider '

'` while `/api/status` still reports the provider as configured. Provision the key explicitly into the tenant profile's `.env`, then re-apply the unit so it is installed into the tenant's own home. Use a **dedicated key**, not a copy of yours: the tenant's agent can read its own `.env`, so a shared key is neither independently revocable nor separately visible in the provider's usage view. Hand the file over with a script the operator runs (SKILL.md §10) instead of an inline command. 6. **A system-level unit** (`/etc/systemd/system/…`, `User=`/`Group=`), not `--user`. ## A read-only code tree breaks everything that builds on demand The tenant reads the app tree and can never write it — that is the point — but the app does not know that: several paths **build into that tree on first use**. Each one turns a read-only code grant into a broken feature whose message names neither the cause nor the tree. - **The dashboard's chat page is the one that bites.** It embeds the real TUI over a PTY, and the launcher resolves the bundle in this order: (1) `HERMES_TUI_DIR` holding `dist/entry.js` → run it directly; (2) a bundle shipped inside the package (`hermes_cli/tui_dist/entry.js`) — absent in a git checkout; (3) otherwise `npm install` + esbuild and **rebuild `ui-tui` in place**. A tenant reaches (3), the build dies with `Failed to write to output file: open …/ui-tui/dist/entry.js: permission denied`, and the UI reports only *Chat unavailable*. The owner never sees it: run as the owner, (3) succeeds silently, so this only ever surfaces for the tenant. - **Pin the prebuilt artifact in the unit** so the search cannot reach the build branch: `Environment=HERMES_TUI_DIR=/ui-tui` (the existing `dist/entry.js` is inside the ACL grant, and node from the system prefix is world-executable). Confirm the branch by **calling the launcher**, not by reading it: set the variable, call `_make_tui_argv(, False)`, and require the returned argv to end in `dist/entry.js`. - **Assert the read in `--verify`**, because "the file exists" and "the tenant can read it" differ: `runuser -u -- head -c 1 /ui-tui/dist/entry.js`. A bundle that is missing or unreadable silently re-arms the build path, and the failure reappears in the UI rather than in the verifier. - **Generalize it after granting read-only code**: grep the runtime for other build-on-write steps (asset manifests, compiled style/theme or plugin caches) and either pre-build them as the owner or point the tenant at a prebuilt location through an env var. The signature of a missed one is `permission denied` on a path inside the app tree in the **tenant's journal** — never a message the UI explains. ## Installing it: you have no root, so the operator runs the script The agent has no passwordless sudo and never asks for a password — that is a standing rule, not a limitation to route around. There is no masked password prompt to reach for either; a command-approval dialog authorises *what* runs and never carries the secret. Offer the two safe paths and recommend the first: **the operator runs the script** (the password never leaves their keyboard), or the operator puts it in their own agent env file — which is equivalent to granting the agent sudo and leaves a plaintext secret on disk. Never accept a password in chat and never write one into a config file. - **Make the script worth running unattended.** The operator runs it once and reports "done"; every failure they cannot see costs a full round-trip. Each rule below came from a silent abort: - **Preflight the tools before touching anything**, and name the missing one with its install command: `setfacl`/`getfacl` come from the `acl` package, which a minimal Ubuntu lacks, and a `set -euo pipefail` script dies on first use of it — *after* creating the user, before anything else, printing nothing. Print the dependency and the fix (`缺少依赖: setfacl → sudo apt install -y acl`, in the operator's language) and exit non-zero, before any write. - **Be idempotent.** `useradd` on an existing user aborts the whole script at step 1 on the second run, right when a half-applied state most needs re-running: `id -u >/dev/null 2>&1 || useradd …`, `install -d`/`install -m` for placement, `systemctl reset-failed` before `enable --now`. - **Report state, never infer it.** The credential step must distinguish "staging file present", "already installed", and "nothing yet". A two-branch check that only looks for the staging file announces "no token yet" on a machine where the token is installed and working — so the next run prints mint instructions for a secret that exists, and a re-mint would invalidate the one already verified end to end. - **Have them tee the log to a path you can read:** `sudo ./install.sh --apply 2>&1 | tee /tmp/x.log`. `tee` runs as the invoking user, so the log needs no root, and you verify from the log plus your own unprivileged reads (`systemctl is-enabled/is-active`, `ls -ld` on the credential directory, `getfacl` on the trees, `systemctl show -p NRestarts`). Do not chain the commands with `&&`: when `--apply` stops halfway, the verification output is the most useful thing you can get. - **"Done" is a self-report; read the state back.** Before writing success down, check the markers yourself: unit present and `active`, credential file present (prove its mode from `ls -ld` on the directory — you cannot read the file and should not need to), staging file *gone* (which proves the script reached that step), restart counter not climbing. A partial install looks exactly like a complete one from the operator's side. ## The permission trade-off you must measure, not assume Granting traversal of the owner's home so the tenant can read the code **re-exposes everything in that home that is world-readable — at every depth, not just at the top**. `/home/` was `750` and `~/.hermes` `700`, so a new user genuinely could not read the sessions, memories or credential files; a top-level glance found "a dozen loose files" (backup tarballs, analyses, notes). One `setfacl -m u::x` on the home turned that into a number worth taking: **274,660 readable files**. Every `o+x` subdirectory — second-runtime trees, `.npm-global`, `.venvs`, the app checkout itself — lets the tenant descend, and everything `o+r` underneath comes with it. Three orders of magnitude past what the eye finds is the whole reason the count has to be taken with `find` as the tenant instead of eyeballed. **Order: strip world bits first, grant ACLs second.** 1. `chmod -R o-rwx /home/` — the owner's own access is unaffected (they are the owner), and the tenant loses nothing it is owed, because its access is about to be granted by ACL. 2. `setfacl -m u::x` on **every ancestor** of the two trees it must read (the home *and* the directory between the home and the app/venv), then `setfacl -R -m u::rX` on those trees and `d:u::rX` so files created later inherit the read. 3. Do the ACLs **after** the `chmod`: `chmod` rewrites the ACL mask, so grants applied first can be silently clipped — the tenant then fails to read code you just granted, and it looks like a traversal problem rather than an ordering one. - The default is therefore `ProtectHome=no` + an explicit `InaccessiblePaths=` list of the sensitive directories and `ReadWritePaths=` for the tenant's own home. **Say out loud in the write-up that this list is enumeration-based**: any sensitive directory created elsewhere later must be added again, and the guard is a habit, not a mechanism. - **`InaccessiblePaths=` requires every path it names to exist.** One entry that is absent (a `.ssh` never created) and the unit dies before `ExecStart` with `Failed to set up mount namespacing: … No such file or directory` and `Main process exited, code=exited, status=226/NAMESPACE` — a start failure that reads like a broken binary rather than a bad path list. Prefix each entry with `-` (`InaccessiblePaths=-/home//.ssh …`) to mean "hide it if it exists", which is what the list was always meant to say. With `Restart=on-failure` the unit then loops forever, so `--apply` should run `systemctl reset-failed ` before `enable --now`. - The stronger shape (`ProtectHome=yes` + re-exposing the code with `BindReadOnlyPaths=`) is the one to reach for when the code can be moved out of `/home` — but systemd does not document a guaranteed ordering between `ProtectHome` and the bind options, so do not enable it on faith. If you use it, the verification below is what tells you whether the code is still reachable. - Copying the app to `/opt` instead of binding it sidesteps the ordering question but duplicates a virtualenv, whose shebangs and `pyvenv.cfg` carry absolute paths from the original location. ## Verify by pretending to be the tenant, in both directions Configuration that *looks* right is the failure mode this whole exercise exists to avoid, so the installer ships a `--verify` mode that runs each probe **as the tenant user** and prints ✓/✗ against the expected answer: cannot read the owner's session DB, memory directory, CLI token directory, or the loose files in the home; can read its own home; can execute the runtime. - **Enumerate; do not spot-check.** Named-path probes only test the paths you happened to think of — the leak above was found *by* one named probe failing while its neighbours looked fine, and a hand-rolled simulator of "what can another user read" will also miss things (it read mode bits and ignored the ACL that granted the traversal). Add a census to `--verify`: as the tenant, `find /home/ -type f -readable -not -path '/*' -not -path '/*' | wc -l` and require **0**, printing the first few offenders when it is not. "How many things can it read outside the two trees" is an answerable question; "is it blocked" is not. - **`--verify` must require root.** `runuser` fails for an unprivileged caller, so every probe prints "refused" — byte-identical to a working boundary, having measured nothing. Check `id -u` and exit non-zero, in the same spirit as the missing-subject check below and the plan-mode rule above. - **The verifier must refuse to run when its subject does not exist.** Otherwise "user not created" and "access denied" print the same word and the check reports a boundary that is not there. This is the general shape: *a check whose failure mode and whose not-applicable mode look identical is not evidence.* - **A plan/dry-run mode must be runnable without root** — refusing to show the plan to a non-root caller removes the one moment where the change is still free to review. - **State what the boundary still does not buy**, from the vendor's own wording: these controls *"do not sandbox a hostile or compromised agent"*, and the owner of the tenant's own machine is root there, so on *their* box the allow-list is self-restraint plus a ledger, not a boundary. ## Where the tenant's artifacts land, and who can open them The tenant *will* produce files (charts, documents, converted media) — that is the point of giving it execution. Three separate things decide whether the operator ever sees them, and each one is measured rather than assumed. - **The working directory is the unit's, not the profile's.** `terminal.cwd` in the tenant's config loses to the session's cwd record, which is the *process* cwd at spawn (`tools/code_execution_env.py::_resolve_child_cwd` resolves session record → registered override → `TERMINAL_CWD` → `os.getcwd()` → staging dir). Omit `WorkingDirectory=` and systemd supplies `/`: every terminal command and every code-kernel cell starts in `/`, `/` is not writable by the tenant, and the agent improvises into `$HOME` — the tell is a report sentence like "the shell's cwd is `/`, so I created it under `$HOME`". Fix in the unit (`WorkingDirectory=/workspace`), assert with `systemctl show -p WorkingDirectory --value`, and put the chosen directory in the tenant's own instruction layer so it stops inventing one per session. - **Whether an image can be *shown* is a property of the client, not of the agent.** The browser entry is the real TUI over a PTY, and the TUI platform hint documents that `MEDIA:` is **not intercepted** there (it prints as literal text) and that a file is delivered by stating its absolute path — so "it just gives me paths" is the instructed behaviour. The desktop client sets `source: 'desktop'` on every session, which is what flips the hint and makes `MEDIA:` render; in remote mode the app then reads the file **from the tenant's machine** through `/api/fs/read-data-url` (the `/api/media` route is deliberately restricted to media roots and is not the path remote clients use). Conclusion to hand the operator: to get inline pictures, change the entry point; to stay on the browser, open the dashboard's Files pane (its root is the tenant's home and the path is editable) or reach the output directory from the OS. - **The reverse-direction ACL is part of the handoff.** A 0700 tenant home blocks the owner too — from Windows, `\\wsl.localhost\\var\lib\` answers "you may not have permission to use this network resource" even though the owner owns the machine. Grant `setfacl -m u::rx ` and `setfacl -R -m u::rX /workspace`: the boundary that must hold is "tenant cannot read owner", and this is the opposite direction, so it costs nothing. The tenant keeps the only write access; its 0600 files (`state.db`, `config.yaml`, `.env`) stay unreadable because the file's own mode outranks the traversal ACL. - **Check the probe's identity, not just its wording.** These verifiers run their probes *as the tenant*, so an owner-side claim written with the same helper silently measures the tenant reading its own files and prints ✓. Write it as `runuser -u -- …` and pair it with the negative: owner lists the workspace, owner still cannot read `state.db`. A probe that cannot fail is not evidence. ## The census is only as wide as the region you named The `find /home/` count reaching 0 says nothing about the rest of the filesystem, and the rest of the filesystem on a workstation with a Windows drive mounted is the larger surface. - **`ProtectSystem=strict` blocks *writes*, not reads — a drvfs/`/mnt/` mount is fully readable to the tenant.** Mount permissions come from the host OS (typically 777, with metadata off), so the tenant can read every KB checkout, note and credential file that lives on the Windows side, and hiding `/home/` changed none of it. Enumerate mounts before claiming a read boundary, and say which regions the census covered. - **Do not reach for `InaccessiblePaths=` on that mount without costing the tenant's own dependencies** — the knowledge-base client in this setup lives on the same drive, so hiding the mount removes the KB as well. Present the real options (re-mount with a narrower expose, relocate the client, accept and document) instead of silently breaking a working feature. - **A behavioural switch in the tenant's `.env` survives the config that shadows it.** With `terminal.backend: local` present in `config.yaml`, an old `TERMINAL_ENV=ssh` line in `.env` is invisible — but delete or reformat that one config key and the env value becomes the effective backend, i.e. a tenant that can no longer execute anything (or, in the other direction, one that executes somewhere you did not intend). Remove leftovers rather than leaving them shadowed, and remember the deploy script copies `.env` verbatim: a fix in the source profile is not live until the next `--apply` plus restart. ## Executing on a Windows guest machine When the tenant's own machine is Windows, the server-side allow-list machinery does not exist: - Microsoft documents **only a handful** of `sshd_config` directives for Windows OpenSSH (`AllowUsers`/`DenyUsers`/`AllowGroups`/`DenyGroups`, `AuthorizedKeysFile` caveats, `GSSAPIAuthentication`). `Match`, `ForceCommand` and `ChrootDirectory` get no Windows coverage, and `ChrootDirectory` is documented as **SFTP-only** — *"A remote session into cmd.exe doesn't honor ChrootDirectory."* Do not design around them on Windows. - The mechanism that does exist is the **default shell**, set in the registry (`HKLM\SOFTWARE\OpenSSH` → `DefaultShell`): point it at your own entry program and put the allow-list inside that program. - Use a **dedicated standard (non-administrator) local account**; an administrator account takes the `administrators_authorized_keys` branch, which requires its ACL to hold only `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` and `BUILTIN\Administrators`. - Auditing: process-creation events (4688) with the group policy that includes the command line. ## The allow-list itself (either platform) - **Allow action names, never binary paths.** A permitted interpreter, archiver, pager, editor, VCS or transfer tool is arbitrary command execution with extra steps — sudo's manual concedes that restricting users to programs without shell escapes *"is often unworkable"*, and GTFOBins is the catalogue of those escapes. Validate with `shlex` into a fixed argv, `shell=False`, no string concatenation, and reject shell metacharacters and path escapes in arguments. - **Quotas have no off-the-shelf SSH equivalent.** The closest hard counter is systemd's `StartLimitIntervalSec=`/`StartLimitBurst=` against a *fixed* unit name per action; anything else is a self-built ledger, and its read-decide-write cycle must be atomic (a lock or a single transaction) or concurrent requests double-spend. All of them are soft limits — the cloud vendors document their own quotas as targets, not ceilings — so present quota as self-restraint plus traceability, not as a defense. - **Log the requested command yourself.** `sshd` records authentication and session events, not what the client asked to run; raising `LogLevel` to `DEBUG` for it is officially discouraged. The wrapper's own structured log plus the host's exec auditing plus a copy off the box is the trio — and the copy is the part that survives the tenant editing the local log. ## The loopback namespace is shared by every tenant on the box A service bound to `127.0.0.1` is private only while there is *one* tenant. Once a second one runs on the same machine, "localhost" is a shared namespace and every service whose design assumes "loopback = only me" is a cross-tenant surface. Measured here before anything was fixed: a **credential-free** `POST` to the owner's own agent A2A port returned a completed task and a real reply, because the runtime documents that posture as *"No token ⇒ localhost only"* — true for one tenant, false from the moment there are two. The filesystem work in this file buys nothing if the tenant can simply call the owner's services over the network. - **Audit it before believing any isolation claim:** enumerate the listening sockets (`ss -ltnp`) and send **one credential-free request to each**, recording the status. The ones that answer or execute are surfaces; the ones returning `401`/`403` prove their own gate and need nothing. A write-up that says "loopback-only" without this table is a guess. - **Expect a zero-auth local daemon in the list** — a local model server answering `/api/tags` to anyone is the usual find. That is a resource/cost exposure rather than a data one; name it rather than leaving it unmentioned. - **Fix per owned surface, or remove the premise.** Give an unprotected service a credential (for a peer runtime: a peer-token map plus a trusted-peers allow-list, with the token read out of the other runtime's own env file so it never enters the conversation). The structural fix is a **per-tenant loopback address**: bind the tenant's dependency on `127.0.0.2` and give the tenant's unit `IPAddressDeny=127.0.0.0/8` + `IPAddressAllow=127.0.0.2/32`, which removes every `127.0.0.1` service at once with no per-service credential to maintain. Its cost is real and worth stating: the tenant's own inbound listener must move off `.1` too, and `tailscale serve` proxies **only** `http://127.0.0.1`, so a loopback-address bridge (`systemd-socket-proxyd`) has to sit in front of the entry path. - **Prove the fix in both directions from one probe:** no credential → `401`, and the peer's own credential → accepted/completed. Only the second answer shows you did not lock out the working integration. The runtime's audit log is the corroboration: the caller's identity string changes from `ip:` to the authenticated peer name, i.e. it is now *identified* rather than *assumed*. ## Quotas for the runtime's own tool calls For a tenant that runs *as an agent*, the SSH-side quota story above is not the one that gets used — its tool calls happen in-process. Ship the gate as a `pre_tool_call` shell hook declared in the tenant profile's own config. - **`fail_closed: true` is mandatory and not the default.** A shell hook that crashes, times out, or prints non-JSON is *fail-open*; that is right for observability and wrong for a gate. With it, even a deleted hook script becomes a refusal. - **Give it three independent ceilings** (per day, per session, per rolling minute) — they catch different failures: cost, one runaway conversation, and a loop. Refused calls must not count. - **A short-lived process doing read-modify-write needs a lock** (`O_CREAT|O_EXCL` plus stale-lock reclaim) or concurrent calls overwrite each other and the count silently under-reports. And **an unreadable state file must be treated as failure, never as "zero used today"** — a sentinel of "empty" is how a quota becomes decorative. - **Keep the thresholds in an override file inside the tenant's home** so the operator can change them without editing code. - **Narrow the tool surface as well, and say which layer is the boundary.** A borrowed runtime has no business with scheduled-job or desktop-control tools: they leave persistent state on the owner's machine or drive their desktop. Configure the toolsets off **and** keep the hook as a second layer that catches a later re-enable. - **Verify the gate as the tenant, and verify the deployment separately.** Run the hook script *as the tenant user* with synthetic payloads for both answers (a banned tool → a block directive, a normal tool → no directive), then confirm the running service is newer than its config (`enable --now` on a live unit is a no-op — see `patching-live-services`). A green file-on-disk check is not evidence that the gate is in the request path.

# Updating the OpenClaw runtime (npm global install)

Measured on this box: install kind `package`, mode `npm`, root
`~/.npm-global/lib/node_modules/openclaw`, channel `stable` (default), service
`openclaw-gateway.service` whose `ExecStart` points straight at
`<root>/dist/index.js`. Config `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json` holds hand-edited
routing, channels and model declarations — back it up before touching anything.

## Procedure

1. `openclaw --version` and `openclaw update status` — channel, available
   version, install kind. `npm view openclaw dist-tags --json` shows the
   candidate tags (`latest`, `extended-stable`, `beta`) independently.
2. `cp ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json.bak-before-update-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)`.
3. `openclaw update --dry-run --yes` — prints the exact planned steps without
   writing (package manager target, plugin sync, completion refresh, service
   restart + doctor).
4. `openclaw update --yes` and then judge it by state, not by its exit output
   (see below).
5. `openclaw update repair --yes --json` if doctor/update reported abandoned
   handoff or post-update convergence warnings.
6. Verify (all four): `openclaw --version` = target; `systemctl --user is-active
   openclaw-gateway` = active; `openclaw channels status` shows each channel
   `running, connected`; `openclaw doctor` runs to completion.

## Traps, each one observed

- **A CLI `openclaw update` run from inside/next to the gateway returns
  `status: skipped`, `reason: managed-service-handoff-started` — that is not a
  failure.** The update is re-parented to a detached supervisor because the
  gateway cannot replace its own package and then kill itself. Real progress
  goes to `/tmp/openclaw-update-run-handoff-*/handoff.log`; the gateway is
  deliberately parked (`inactive`) mid-update and restarted at the end
  (`Restarted systemd service: openclaw-gateway.service`). Track it with the log
  plus `openclaw update status --json` → `lastRun.status: succeeded`,
  `lastRun.target.version`, `lastRun.after.version`, `availability.available`.
- **A stale `~/.openclaw/.upgrading` file (contents = a PID that no longer
  exists) poisons the next update.** Symptoms: `existing managed handoff lease is
  incompatible; retain diagnostics and run openclaw triage manually` and, from
  doctor, `Update executor was lost during native preparation`. Confirm the PID
  is gone (`ps -p <pid>`) and move the file aside — archive it, do not delete —
  then run `openclaw update repair --yes`.
- **Doctor and `update repair` fail with `SQLite source did not stabilize after
  10 read-only inspection attempts` when the gateway is hot** (it is writing its
  own state DB). Wait 1–2 minutes and re-run; do not conclude the DB is broken.
- **CLI-side doctor reports `channels.a2a.peers.hermes.token: env var
  "A2A_HERMES_TOKEN" … feature unavailable`.** False alarm from the CLI shell:
  the token lives in the systemd drop-in `EnvironmentFile`
  (`~/.config/systemd/user/openclaw-gateway.service.d/a2a-hermes.env`), which the
  gateway loads and the interactive CLI does not. `openclaw channels status`
  showing `A2A default: … connected` settles the question.
- **Plaintext-secret and `models[].route` doctor warnings are pre-existing
  config debt, not update fallout.** They appear identically before and after;
  do not treat the update as the cause and do not "fix" them mid-update.
- **Transcript-archive warnings during migration** (`Missing canonical
  transcript archive copy …` / `historical_transcript_deferred`) are historical:
  the SQLite blobs are retained and migration completes; they are only a problem
  if a conversation a human expects is actually missing.
- **Schedule the update inside the awake window (23:00–06:00 is a hard power
  cutoff on this box).** The restart is not instant and a cut mid-update leaves
  exactly the half-finished handoff described above.
